title: Big Tech's AI Spending Hits $760 Billion as Cloud Revenue Finally Accelerates
excerpt: Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta are pouring record sums into AI infrastructure, but Q2 earnings show cloud and AI revenue growth is starting to catch up with the massive outlays.
body:
• The four largest tech companies are on track to spend a combined $760 billion on AI infrastructure in 2026, up from $413 billion in 2025, with Q2 capital expenditure alone reaching $170 billion.
  • Google Cloud revenue surged 82% year-over-year to $24.8 billion in Q2, while Amazon Web Services grew 37% to $42.2 billion — its fastest pace in 18 quarters.
  • Alphabet recorded its first-ever negative free cash flow, burning $5.9 billion in the quarter despite strong revenue growth, and raised its full-year capex guidance to $195–$205 billion.
  • Investors remain divided: cloud revenue is accelerating, but cash flows are under historic pressure as companies prioritize capacity over near-term profitability.

The second-quarter earnings season has crystallized an emerging reality for Big Tech's artificial intelligence bet: the spending is enormous and still growing, but the revenue it generates is finally starting to inflect upward.

Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta collectively spent $170 billion on capital expenditure between April and June, up 72% from a year earlier, and are on track for a combined $760 billion in full-year AI spending, according to FactSet estimates cited by Statista. That figure stood at just $413 billion in 2025.

Cloud Growth Steals the Show

The quarter's standout was Google Cloud, which posted $24.8 billion in revenue, an 82% year-over-year increase that handily beat the $22.5 billion analysts had expected. The acceleration — from 45% growth in Q1 and 39% in Q4 2025 — marked a clear inflection in demand for AI computing infrastructure.

"Our AI investments are redefining what's possible across every part of our business. Google Cloud revenues accelerated to 82% growth, driven by demand for AI infrastructure and AI solutions."

— Sundar Pichai, CEO of Alphabet

Google's cloud order backlog jumped to $514 billion, up from $460 billion in the prior quarter, providing visibility into future revenue as new data centers come online. Alphabet also disclosed that it would lease AI data center capacity from third parties to meet demand, even at the cost of lower margins.

Amazon Web Services delivered $42.2 billion in quarterly revenue, growing 37% — its fastest expansion in more than four years. The AI segment within AWS showed triple-digit growth, reaching an annualized revenue of $25 billion. Microsoft's Azure cloud business grew 43%, ahead of forecasts, while paid seats for its Copilot AI assistant surpassed 30 million.

The Cash Flow Reckoning

The revenue acceleration, however, has not been enough to offset the sheer scale of spending. Alphabet reported its first negative free cash flow on record, burning $5.9 billion in Q2, and raised its full-year capex guidance to a range of $195 billion to $205 billion. Chief Financial Officer Anat Ashkenazi indicated the cash burn trend would persist over coming quarters.

The pattern extends across the group. Amazon's trailing 12-month free cash flow swung to an outflow of $7.6 billion from an inflow of $18.2 billion a year earlier. Meta's free cash flow fell to $784 million as costs climbed 55% year-over-year, even as revenue rose 28% to $60.8 billion. Microsoft's annual free cash flow is expected to roughly halve to $25.4 billion.

Capex-to-revenue ratios have nearly doubled across the board. Meta's ratio is projected to hit 54.9%, up from 35.9% a year ago. Alphabet's climbed to 41% from 23%, Microsoft's to 45% from 31%, and Amazon's to 25% from 18%.

Investors Split on the Signal

Markets have responded unevenly. Alphabet fell about 5% after its results despite strong revenue beats, with investors focused on the capex hike. Amazon's stock rose on its earnings despite higher spending guidance, boosted by the AWS acceleration. Microsoft initially rallied on Azure growth before giving back gains as analysts scrutinized the second-half spending trajectory.

"This is the deepest industrywide capex cycle they have had," said Justin Post, internet analyst at Bank of America. "They see it as a once in a lifetime opportunity."

The competitive dynamics are intensifying. Google Cloud's rapid gains are pressuring AWS and Azure, while Meta has entered talks to rent computing power to Anthropic, expanding into a cloud-like business without a traditional cloud platform.

What's Next

The four hyperscalers are collectively on track to spend $1.5 trillion on data centers across 2026 and 2027, according to FactSet. With AI model training and inference demand remaining supply-constrained, analysts expect capex to continue climbing even as the companies lean on debt issuance and equity sales to fund the build-out. The central question for investors remains whether AI revenue can grow faster than the capital needed to generate it.
nri_angle: The AI spending race among U.S. tech giants has broad implications for the global technology workforce and investment landscape.
author: Diaspora Desk
